Getting started with gtropic

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

This vignette walks through installing the gtropic package, retrieving your first G-TROPIC dataset, and understanding what comes back.

What is G-TROPIC?

G-TROPIC is a multi-exposure, live (updated weekly) dataset spanning global tropical storms from 1980 onward, combining IBTrACS storm track data, GHSL population rasters, geoBoundaries ADM2 administrative units, Groundsource flood polygons, and ERA5-Land precipitation. G-TROPIC adheres to FAIR data principles and is publicly available via Harvard Dataverse, with versioned updates that incorporate recent storm and precipitation data once a week. At second-level administrative unit (ADM2) resolution worldwide for compatibility with health outcome and other data, G-TROPIC provides population totals and population-weighted centroids, storm exposure metrics from both best-track and wind-radii methods, flood exposure metrics, and daily local precipitation totals, along with ADM2 metadata for region and WHO classifications.

For enhanced accessibility, we developed this open-source R package, gtropic, for easy retrieval, exploration, and mapping of G-TROPIC data directly in R.

Installation

The development version of gtropic can be installed from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("sparklabnyc/gtropic")

gtropic can then be loaded and attached in your current R session as usual with:

library(gtropic)

Data availability

Let’s get oriented by running some of the gtropic helper functions that let us know what G-TROPIC data is available in the first place. Doing so will help us define the specific query we later send to the G-TROPIC database, so we can retrieve only the data we need, and nothing more (to save on memory and disk space).

We can examine the available years of data using:

gtropic_years()
#> $historical
#>  [1] 1980 1981 1982 1983 1984 1985 1986 1987 1988 1989 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994
#> [16] 1995 1996 1997 1998 1999 2000 2001 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009
#> [31] 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
#> [46] 2025
#>
#> $current
#> [1] 2026
#>
#> $all
#>  [1] 1980 1981 1982 1983 1984 1985 1986 1987 1988 1989 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994
#> [16] 1995 1996 1997 1998 1999 2000 2001 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009
#> [31] 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
#> [46] 2025 2026

adm2s <- gtropic_adm2()

For example, let’s look at a few available WHO_ENTITYs shipped in G-TROPIC:

head(unique(adm2s$WHO_ENTITY))
#> [1] "Afghanistan"    "United Kingdom" "Albania"        "Algeria"
#> [5] "United States"  NA

Or, for instance, the available administrative units in a specific country:

gtropic_adm2(WHO_ENTITY = "United States")

Similarly, we can also get a list of all the available storms in the dataset. By default, gtropic_storms() returns all storms from 1980 onward, but if we pass in a year, then we can get the list of storms for that given year:

gtropic_storms(year = 2025)
#> # A tibble: 77 × 4
#>    STORM_ID      STORM_NAME   USA_ATCF_ID STORM_GENESIS_DATE_UTC
#>    <chr>         <chr>        <chr>       <date>
#>  1 2025017S18122 Sean-2025    SH102025    2025-01-17
#>  2 2025024S11082 Faida-2025   SH112025    2025-01-23
#>  3 2025029S25043 Elvis-2025   SH122025    2025-01-28
#>  4 2025034S19166 Unnamed-2025 SH152025    2025-02-02
#>  5 2025039S14125 Zelia-2025   SH172025    2025-02-08
#>  6 2025052S14148 Alfred-2025  SH182025    2025-02-21
#>  7 2025052S23038 Honde-2025   SH232025    2025-02-21
#>  8 2025054S13182 Rae-2025     SH192025    2025-02-22
#>  9 2025054S17051 Garance-2025 SH222025    2025-02-23
#> 10 2025056S16171 Seru-2025    SH212025    2025-02-24
#> # ℹ 67 more rows

The STORM_GENESIS_DATE_UTC column in that last result is the date used by every temporal filter in the package. So, for example, if you inquire after storms from 2025, the package is designed to return storms whose genesis date (UTC) occurs within the 2025 calendar year. For more in depth discussion, see the “Selecting storms by date” section below, and the filtering vignette.

One of the most important pieces of metadata is the G-TROPIC codebook, which can be obtained with:

cb <- gtropic_codebook()
names(cb)
#> [1] "codebook_version" "format"           "created_for"      "read_in_r"
#> [5] "notes"            "raw_sources"      "datasets"

The returned codebook object contains all the information needed to understand the retrieved datasets, including but not limited to their columns, what those columns measure, and the original provenance of the data, both in terms of the raw data sources, as well as the G-TROPIC backend pipeline scripts that generated that data.

Related to the codebook is the gtropic_exposures() function, which lists the variable names associated with exposures available in G-TROPIC, their units of measurement, their default aggregation methods (for plotting exposure maps), and whether or not the gtropic_plot() function supports plotting the exposure.

gtropic_exposures()
#> $wind
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   metric                      label               unit  aggregate plot_supported
#>   <chr>                       <chr>               <chr> <chr>     <lgl>

#> 2 VMAX_GUST_MS                Maximum wind gust … m/s   max       TRUE
#> 3 SUST_DUR_MINUTES            Sustained wind dur… minu… max       TRUE
#> 4 GUST_DUR_MINUTES            Wind gust duration… minu… max       TRUE
#> 5 WIND_RADII_VMAX_SUST_MS     Wind radii sustain… m/s   max       TRUE
#> 6 WIND_RADII_SUST_DUR_MINUTES Wind radii duratio… minu… max       TRUE
#>
#> $precip
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   metric    label              unit  aggregate plot_supported

#>
#> $flood

A first query

The cornerstone function of the gtropic package is the gtropic_data() function. Let’s start by using it to retrieve all available G-TROPIC data impacting ADM2s inside the United States, for those storms forming in calendar year 2025:

usa_25 <- gtropic_data(
  WHO_ENTITY = "United States",
  date_range = c(2025, 2025)
)
#> Discovering datasets in collection "gtropic".
#> Retrieving 7 files (166.0 MB) ; 3 already cached.
#> Downloading '02_wind/exposures/2025.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/zero_pairs/2025.parquet'.
#> Downloading '04_precip/2025.parquet'.
#> Downloading '03_flood/2025.parquet'.
#> Downloading '01_pop/2025.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/storm_tracks/2025.parquet'.
#> Downloading 'metadata/adm2_geometry_simplified.parquet'.

usa_25
#>
#> ── G-TROPIC data ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Historical dataset: doi:10.70122/FK2/SWEYST (version 4.0)
#> • Genesis dates: "2025-01-01" to "2025-12-31"
#> • Storms: 10
#> • ADM2 units: 803
#>
#> ── Tables
#> • wind: 1068 rows x 12 columns
#> • precip: 4272 rows x 3 columns
#> • flood: 661 rows x 7 columns
#> • zero_pairs: 225182 rows x 5 columns
#> • tracks: 682 rows x 10 columns
#> • pop: 803 rows x 6 columns
#> • storm_metadata: 10 rows x 4 columns
#> • adm2: 803 rows x 5 columns
#> • geometry: 803 rows x 2 columns
#> • codebook: 7 entries (list)
#> • links: 1068 rows x 12 columns
#>
#> ℹ Use `summary()` for detail.

Printing the result gives a compact summary: which version of the data you retrieved, the span of storm genesis dates, how many storms and administrative units were selected based on your filters, and the size of each table returned.

But, for more detail, including resolved filter settings and any warnings raised, we can use:

summary(usa_25)
#>
#> ── G-TROPIC data summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
#> ── Sources ──
#>
#> • Server: "demo.dataverse.org"
#> • Historical dataset: doi:10.70122/FK2/SWEYST v4.0
#> • Files retrieved: 10 (166.8 MB)
#> • Retrieved at: 2026-10-30 22:50:44 UTC
#>
#> ── Tables ──
#>
#> • wind: 1068 rows x 12 columns
#> • precip: 4272 rows x 3 columns
#> • flood: 661 rows x 7 columns
#> • zero_pairs: 225182 rows x 5 columns
#> • tracks: 682 rows x 10 columns
#> • pop: 803 rows x 6 columns
#> • storm_metadata: 10 rows x 4 columns
#> • adm2: 803 rows x 5 columns
#> • geometry: 803 rows x 2 columns
#> • codebook: 7 entries (list)
#> • links: 1068 rows x 12 columns
#>
#> ── Resolved filters ──
#>
#> • ADM2 units: 803
#> • Storms: 10
#> • Genesis window: 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31
#> • Wind radius: 500 km
#> • Precipitation window: -2/ +1 days within 500 km
#> • Flood window: -2/+1 days within 500 km (match: "start")

The summary() function here shows the important resolved filters used by the data query we just sent, revealing some default argument values used by the gtropic_data() function:

  1. The wind_radius_km argument, which by default is 500km, defining a spatial wind field of interest. This restricts the function to return wind exposure data associated with storm tracks that come within 500km of any ADM2. Combined with our passed in values for WHO_ENTITY and date_range, this means we are asking for wind exposure data for storms formed in the calendar year 2025 that come within 500km of any ADM2 in the United States.

  2. Similarly, separate precip_radius_km and flood_radius_km arguments define spatial precipitation and flood fields, in order to link precipitation and flood data to storm tracks. By default, these are both also 500km.

  3. The precip_days_before and precip_days_after arguments (along with flood_days_before and flood_days_after) define the temporal windows linking precipitation and flood data to storm tracks. By default, G-TROPIC will assume you want daily precipitation and flood data starting 2 days before and ending up to 1 day after a storm track makes its closest approach with an ADM2.

Note that the radius_km arguments can be any integer in the range (0, “Inf”], or NULL. Passing in “Inf” or NULL does not impose a spatial field on any storm track, and returns all available wind/precip/flood data.

The precip/flood_days_before/after arguments can be any whole number in the range [0, “Inf”).

The gtropic_data object

A gtropic_data object is just a named list of data frames, behaving like any other named list:

names(usa_25)
#>  [1] "wind"           "precip"         "flood"          "zero_pairs"
#>  [5] "tracks"         "pop"            "storm_metadata" "adm2"
#>  [9] "geometry"       "codebook"       "links"
usa_25$wind
#> # A tibble: 1,068 × 12
#>    ADM2_ID  STORM_ID LOCAL_DATETIME_STORM…¹ LOCAL_DATETIME_MAX_W…² STORM_DIST_KM
#>    <chr>    <chr>    <chr>                  <chr>                          <dbl>
#>  1 5242332… 2025185… 2025-07-06T14:00:00-0… 2025-07-06T05:00:00-0…         152.
#>  2 5242332… 2025223… 2025-08-16T22:00:00-0… 2025-08-16T22:15:00-0…         196.
#>  3 5242332… 2025280… 2025-10-10T07:15:00-0… 2025-10-10T09:45:00-0…         277.
#>  4 5242332… 2025185… 2025-07-07T09:45:00-0… 2025-07-07T13:45:00-0…          11.4
#>  5 5242332… 2025215… 2025-08-02T14:00:00-0… 2025-08-02T15:00:00-0…         471.
#>  6 5242332… 2025243… 2025-09-09T19:30:00-1… 2025-09-09T20:45:00-1…         311.
#>  7 5242332… 2025185… 2025-07-07T14:00:00-0… 2025-07-07T12:45:00-0…          75.1
#>  8 5242332… 2025185… 2025-07-07T14:00:00-0… 2025-07-07T12:30:00-0…         108.
#>  9 5242332… 2025185… 2025-07-04T08:15:00-0… 2025-07-06T04:00:00-0…         358.
#> 10 5242332… 2025185… 2025-07-07T00:15:00-0… 2025-07-07T03:00:00-0…          77.9
#> # ℹ 1,058 more rows
#> # ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​LOCAL_DATETIME_STORM_CLOSEST, ²​LOCAL_DATETIME_MAX_WIND
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: VMAX_SUST_MS <dbl>, SUST_DUR_MINUTES <dbl>,
#> #   VMAX_GUST_MS <dbl>, GUST_DUR_MINUTES <dbl>, WIND_RADII_VMAX_SUST_MS <dbl>,
#> #   WIND_RADII_SUST_DUR_MINUTES <dbl>, LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST <chr>

By default, the gtropic_data() function returns:

  • wind: one row per ADM2 per storm, for those ADM2s within the specified wind_radius_km of a storm track, for those ADM2-storm pairs where wind exposure was non-zero. This is the core exposure table.
  • precip – one row per ADM2 per local calendar date, for those ADM2s within the specified precip_radius_km of a storm track, and for dates falling within precip_days_before and precip_days_after the local date of a storm track’s closest approach to that ADM2 (i.e., for the temporal window defined by LOCAL_DATETIME_STORM_CLOSEST - precip_days_before through LOCAL_DATETIME_STORM_CLOSEST + precip_days_after).
  • flood – one row per observed flood event, for flood events whose FLOOD_START_DATE falls within flood_days_before and flood_days_after the LOCAL_DATETIME_STORM_CLOSEST, for those ADM2s within flood_radius_km of a storm track.
  • pop – population and population-weighted centroid data, per ADM2 per year.
  • adm2 – the lookup table of ADM2s.
  • codebook – the dataset’s own documentation, as a nested list.
  • zero_pairs – ADM2-storm pairs with no measurable wind.
  • tracks – raw storm-track observations for those storms coming within max(c(wind_radius_km, precip_radius_km, flood_radius_km)) of any of the requested ADM2s.
  • geometry – ADM2 boundaries, as an sf object.
  • storm_metadata – storm names, identifiers, and genesis dates.
  • links – see below.

If you are on a tighter computational budget and would like to reduce file transfer and storage requirements, pass only the tables required for your analysis through the tables argument.

The links table

links is returned whenever any storm-linked table is. It has one row per ADM2-storm pair retained by the union of the fields for the requested hazard tables (or all selected pairs when every requested field is unbounded):

usa_25$links
#> # A tibble: 1,068 × 12
#>    STORM_ID      ADM2_ID      LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLO…¹ STORM_DIST_KM WIND_EXPOSURE
#>    <chr>         <chr>        <date>                         <dbl> <lgl>
#>  1 2025185N30280 52423323B10… 2025-07-06                     152.  TRUE
#>  2 2025223N17337 52423323B10… 2025-08-16                     196.  TRUE
#>  3 2025280N11319 52423323B10… 2025-10-10                     277.  TRUE
#>  4 2025185N30280 52423323B10… 2025-07-07                      11.4 TRUE
#>  5 2025215N33284 52423323B10… 2025-08-02                     471.  TRUE
#>  6 2025243N14239 52423323B10… 2025-09-09                     311.  TRUE
#>  7 2025185N30280 52423323B10… 2025-07-07                      75.1 TRUE
#>  8 2025185N30280 52423323B10… 2025-07-07                     108.  TRUE
#>  9 2025185N30280 52423323B10… 2025-07-04                     358.  TRUE
#> 10 2025185N30280 52423323B10… 2025-07-07                      77.9 TRUE
#> # ℹ 1,058 more rows
#> # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: WIND_IN_FIELD <lgl>, PRECIP_IN_FIELD <lgl>,
#> #   PRECIP_WINDOW_START <date>, PRECIP_WINDOW_END <date>, FLOOD_IN_FIELD <lgl>,
#> #   FLOOD_WINDOW_START <date>, FLOOD_WINDOW_END <date>

A few important columns include:

  • LOCAL_DATE_STORM_CLOSEST: the local calendar date on which the storm passed closest to that unit. This is used to anchor both precipitation and flooding windows (e.g. if you request precipitation data for an ADM2 on the 2 days before and 2 days after a given storm, then the temporal window is calculated with respect to this date).
  • STORM_DIST_KM: how close the corresponding storm came to the corresponding ADM2 (in kilometers).
  • WIND_EXPOSURE: whether the pair had measurable wind (TRUE) or not (FALSE).
  • WIND_IN_FIELD, PRECIP_IN_FIELD, and FLOOD_IN_FIELD: whether the ADM2 was close enough to the storm track to be considered for wind, precipitation and flooding data inclusion, respectively.

The links table helps avoid duplicating precipitation/flooding rows for every storm returned in a query. For instance, a single rainy day in one ADM2 may land inside two storms’ spatio-temporal windows; returning that day twice would cause problems if the PRECIP_MM exposure were to be summed later in an analysis. Instead, tidy tables are returned along with the links table, and we leave the join operations necessary for your analysis to you, the user. The linkage vignette details this in full.

How to inspect your query’s metadata

Three functions provide access to the metadata pertaining to your gtropic_data object:

# Exactly which files were retrieved, at which version
gtropic_manifest(usa_25)
#>
#> ── gtropic version manifest ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Server: "demo.dataverse.org"
#> • Historical dataset: doi:10.70122/FK2/SWEYST (version 4.0)
#> • Files recorded: 10
#> • Total size: 166.8 MB
#> • Retrieved: 2026-10-30 22:50:44 UTC
#> • Package version: "0.0.0.9000"
#>
#> ℹ Pass this object as `manifest` to `gtropic_data()` to
#> reproduce the same retrieval.
# The filters as the package resolved them
gtropic_filters(usa_25)

#> "2025308N09145"]

gtropic_availability(usa_25)

The manifest records the published files actually used, including paths, concrete dataset versions, checksums, and each file’s original download time. Saving it lets you reproduce the same retrieval with gtropic_data(manifest = mf), even if :latest has since changed. The versions-and-caching vignette explains canonical replay and cache behavior.

gtropic_availability() records source update schedules, known coverage, and the requested period used for diagnostics. Availability warnings are conditional: for example, a recent wind request can warn about provisional IBTrACS data, a recent precipitation request about the typical ERA5-Land lag, and a flood request reaching or extending beyond 2026-01-22 about the known Groundsource flood endpoint. Inspect gtropic_warnings() to retain these diagnostics with an analysis; availability is metadata, not a guarantee that every record exists.

Larger queries, caching, and size guardrails

Before scaling up your queries or relaxing your filters to download larger portions of the G-TROPIC dataset, it’s worth getting to know how file caching and size guardrails work in gtropic:

The file cache: To save repeated downloads of the same queried data, downloads are kept between sessions using the file cache by default. You can disable caching for the current R session using:

gtropic_cache_disable()

Or bypass it for one query by passing cache = FALSE. To retain a disabled choice across R sessions, use gtropic_cache_disable(persist = TRUE).

The size guardrail: Calling gtropic_data() with no arguments requests all available tables for the full global record. This can require a substantial download. Before downloading anything estimated to be larger than 1GB, gtropic_data() will prompt you to confirm going ahead with the download. In a non-interactive session, for instance a scheduled/scripted job, it will raise an error instead, unless you pass the confirm = FALSE argument.

Both topics are covered extensively in vignette("versions-and-caching").

Summary

  • Use the discovery helpers to identify available years, places, storms, and exposure metrics before making a query.
  • gtropic_data() returns a named collection of exposure tables plus metadata that documents the selected records and source files.
  • Use the links table to connect precipitation and flooding records to storms without duplicating observations, and retain the manifest for reproducibility.

  • vignette("versions-and-caching") walks through reproducibility and download management best practices in gtropic.
  • vignette("plotting") examines how to quickly visualize exposure maps of G-TROPIC data using the gtropic_plot() plotting function.
